title: The Hungarian Revolution, 1956 — students, a radio station, and Stalin's boots
sources: Wikipedia: Hungarian Revolution of 1956 — began 23 October 1956 in Budapest when university students called on the public to join them at the Parliament to protest Soviet domination; a delegation of students entered the Magyar Rádió building to broadcast their sixteen demands but was detained; when protesters outside demanded their release, ÁVH secret police shot several students; the crowd sang the banned National Song; protesters demolished the eight-metre Stalin Monument; the uprising was crushed by Soviet tanks and troops from 4 November; about 200,000 fled Hungary as refugees
Wikipedia: Stalin Monument (Budapest) — demonstrators demolished the Stalin statue, leaving only his boots, in which they planted a Hungarian flag
Wikipedia: Imre Nagy — the reformist prime minister of the revolution
Also on this day (candidates.md, in the app): 1906 Alberto Santos-Dumont flies his 14-bis for 50 metres; 1641 Irish rebels try to seize Dublin Castle
Photos (public domain / CC0): Erika Szeles, a 15-year-old fighter, Budapest 1956 (two photos); collage of the revolution (CC0); a Soviet tank in Budapest, 1956; Imre Nagy; the Hungarian Parliament
Illustrative stock footage (Pexels, free licence; not of the event): a Hungarian flag on a historic building

post.facebook:
On this day in 1956, university students in Budapest called on Hungarians to march for freedom from Soviet control — and began a revolution.

The crowd sang a banned patriotic poem. A delegation of students went into the state radio building to broadcast their sixteen demands, and was detained; when the crowd outside demanded their release, the secret police opened fire. Across the city, protesters pulled down the eight-metre statue of Stalin. Only the boots stayed on the plinth — and they planted a Hungarian flag in them.

For a few days, the revolution seemed to win. Then, on 4 November, Soviet tanks rolled into Budapest. About 200,000 Hungarians fled the country.

Also on 23 October: Santos-Dumont flew his 14-bis (1906), and Irish rebels tried to seize Dublin Castle (1641).

youtube.title: The Night Stalin's Statue Fell — Only His Boots Were Left #Shorts
youtube.description:
23 October 1956: students in Budapest marched for freedom from Soviet control. They tried to broadcast sixteen demands from the state radio and were detained; the secret police fired on the crowd outside. That night protesters pulled down the 8-metre Stalin Monument — only the boots were left, with a Hungarian flag planted in them. The revolution seemed to win for a few days, until Soviet tanks rolled in on 4 November. About 200,000 Hungarians fled.

Also on 23 October: Santos-Dumont's 14-bis flight (1906) and the Irish rising at Dublin Castle (1641).
